notes: Ruling slot 1 holds Velasco Ibarra's Federación Nacional Velasquista (his fifth presidency since Sept 1968). There was no formal coalition: the Radical Liberals (slot 2) were the main 1968 opposition. Conservative Party in slot 14 (agrarian-clerical, starting popularity); Ponce's PSC moved from MD slot 14 to slot 16. CFP in slot 20 (MD places the Bucaram family's later PRE there). Falangist ARNE in slot 21.

0.name: La Junta del 63
0.text:
The Junta of '63 is the network of officers and civilian allies who ran Ecuador from the July 1963 coup until 1966 under Admiral Ramón Castro Jijón. They outlawed the Communist Party, purged the universities and launched a first agrarian reform with American advice under the Alliance for Progress.

They remain convinced that Ecuador needs a disciplined, technocratic military government aligned with Washington to contain Castroism and modernise the country. Discredited by their fall amid protests in 1966, they still have friends in the officer corps and in business, and watch Velasco's chaotic rule with impatience.

1.name: Federación Nacional Velasquista
1.text:
The National Velasquista Federation is the political vehicle of José María Velasco Ibarra, the great orator who has dominated Ecuadorian politics since the 1930s. Elected for the fifth time in June 1968, he governs since September 1968 without a majority in Congress, facing a fiscal crisis, student unrest and constant clashes with the legislature and the courts.

Velasquismo is less a doctrine than a personal bond between the caudillo and the masses, combining Catholic moralism, anti-oligarchic rhetoric and authoritarian impulses. It appeals to the urban poor and the provincial middle classes. Its leverage lies in Velasco's charisma and in his ties to the army, commanded by his nephew, Defence Minister Jorge Acosta Velasco.

2.name: Partido Liberal Radical Ecuatoriano
2.text:
The Radical Liberal Party is the heir of Eloy Alfaro's revolution of 1895, which separated church and state, and it governed Ecuador for much of the first half of the century. Its candidate Andrés F. Córdova came a close second to Velasco in 1968, and it now leads the opposition in Congress.

It defends secular education, civil liberties, constitutional government and economic modernisation, and stands firmly in the Western camp. Its base lies in Guayaquil and the coast, among professionals, merchants and public employees. Younger members around Rodrigo Borja are pressing it toward social democracy.

3.name: Partido Socialista Ecuatoriano
3.text:
The Ecuadorian Socialist Party, founded in 1926, is the oldest party of the Ecuadorian left. After the radical wing broke away in the early 1960s, the remaining party took a moderate course, joining electoral alliances with the Liberals and other progressive forces.

It stands for agrarian reform, labour rights, public education and national control of natural resources within a democratic framework, keeping its distance from both Moscow and Havana. Its base is among teachers, intellectuals, artisans and union members in Quito and the provincial towns, and its leverage lies in its union ties and its role in centre-left alliances.

4.name: Partido Comunista del Ecuador
4.text:
The Communist Party of Ecuador, founded in 1926 and renamed in 1931, is led by its veteran secretary general Pedro Saad, a Guayaquil labour leader. Banned by the 1963 junta, it has regained a precarious legality but remains under police surveillance.

Loyal to Moscow, it rejects guerrilla adventures and Maoist splits in favour of a broad anti-imperialist front, nationalisation of foreign companies, radical agrarian reform and ties with the socialist countries. Its strength lies in the Confederation of Workers of Ecuador (CTE), among indigenous peasant federations of the Sierra and in the universities.

5.name: Federación de Estudiantes Universitarios del Ecuador
5.english: Federation of University Students of Ecuador
5.native_full: Federación de Estudiantes Universitarios del Ecuador
5.text:
The FEUE is the national federation of university students, the most militant force in Ecuadorian politics at the end of the 1960s. Its campaign for free admission led to the massacre at the University of Guayaquil on 29 May 1969, when troops killed students occupying the campus, and it is now in open war with Velasco.

Inspired by Cuba, Che Guevara and the student revolts of 1968, it demands a free and popular university, an end to oligarchic rule and to US influence. Its factions range from Moscow communists to Maoists and Castroists, and its leverage lies in strikes, occupations and street mobilisation.

6.name: Los Garcianos
6.text:
The Garcianos are integrist Catholics of the Sierra who revere Gabriel García Moreno, the nineteenth-century president who consecrated Ecuador to the Sacred Heart. They gather around conservative clergy, Catholic newspapers and old landowning families in Quito, Cuenca and Riobamba.

They reject liberalism, secular education and the Second Vatican Council's reforms, and regard American consumer culture and Protestant missions as a moral invasion. They dream of a confessional Catholic state with a strong ruler. Their leverage is the pulpit and the social authority of the Sierra elite.

7.name: Oficiales Nacionalistas
7.text:
The Nationalist Officers are army colonels and majors who admire General Juan Velasco Alvarado's revolutionary military government in neighbouring Peru. They watch the first oil discoveries in the Oriente by Texaco-Gulf with the conviction that the country's new wealth must not fall to foreign companies and the old oligarchy.

They favour a military government of national reconstruction, state control of oil, agrarian reform and a non-aligned foreign policy at a distance from Washington. Without public organisation, they count on the army's growing disgust with civilian politics and with Velasco's weakness.

8.name: Hijos de Yabal Amil
8.text:
The Sons of Jabal Amil are a few Shia families from southern Lebanon who settled as traders in Guayaquil and Quito among the larger Christian Lebanese community. They meet privately for religious occasions and follow news of Imam Musa al-Sadr's efforts to organise the Lebanese Shia.

They favour a moderate, socially engaged faith that respects their host country's laws and works for the uplift of their community back home. Wholly apolitical in Ecuador, their only leverage lies in business ties and their standing within the Arab-Ecuadorian clubs of the coast.

9.name: Círculo de Nayaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle consists of a handful of young Lebanese Shia in Guayaquil who receive cassette sermons and pamphlets from Najaf, where the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini teaches that the jurists must rule. They read in secret and debate the duty to resist unjust rulers.

They reject both Western capitalism and Soviet communism, condemn the Shah and Israel, and see their elders' discretion as cowardice. In Ecuador they have no mosque, no funds and no audience beyond their own circle, making them a curiosity rather than a force.

10.name: Los Piadosos del Puerto
10.text:
The Pious of the Port are Sunni Palestinian and Syrian merchants of Guayaquil who keep their faith in a city without a mosque, gathering for Friday prayers in homes and back rooms and importing Qurans printed in Saudi Arabia.

They practise a quiet, orthodox Islam that respects the authorities and stays out of Ecuadorian politics, while admiring the Saudi monarchy as guardian of the holy places. Their hope is a recognised Islamic centre funded from the Gulf. Their leverage is limited to commerce and their good relations with local officials.

11.name: Los Estudiantes del Califato
11.text:
The Caliphate Students are a tiny group of Arab students at the Central University in Quito who have read the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir and the writings of Sayyid Qutb, brought back from summers in Lebanon and Jordan.

They denounce Arab nationalism, monarchy and Marxism alike as betrayals of Islam and call for a single caliphate ruling by sharia. Shocked by the defeat of 1967, they argue that only a return to faith can restore the Muslim world. They have no following in Ecuador beyond a few friends and no influence on its politics.

12.name: Los Hermanos de Damasco
12.text:
The Brothers of Damascus are Syrian Muslim émigrés in Guayaquil sympathetic to the Muslim Brotherhood, which the Ba'ath regime has persecuted since 1963. They organise charity, Arabic classes and religious instruction for the children of Muslim families.

They see Islam as a complete social order, favour moral renewal and social justice through religious institutions, and oppose both the Ba'ath and communism. They are few, modest and law-abiding, and their influence reaches no further than a handful of families and their correspondence with Brotherhood exiles in Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

13.name: Junta Nacional de Planificación y Coordinación Económica
13.native_full: Junta Nacional de Planificación y Coordinación Económica
13.text:
JUNAPLA, the National Board for Planning and Economic Coordination, was created in 1954 under the influence of the UN Economic Commission for Latin America. Its economists drafted the development plans of the 1960s and advise every government on budgets, agrarian reform and industry.

Its technocrats believe Ecuador's future depends on planning, import substitution and the rational use of the coming oil revenues, not on caudillos and party quarrels. They favour a strong executive able to override Congress and the regional oligarchies. Their leverage lies in expertise and in the ear of presidents and generals alike.

14.name: Partido Conservador Ecuatoriano
14.text:
The Conservative Party, founded in 1883 as the party of the Church and the Sierra landowners, is one of Ecuador's two historic parties. In 1968 it backed Camilo Ponce Enríquez, who came third, and it now sits in opposition to Velasco, whom it has alternately supported and fought.

It defends the Catholic Church, religious education, the family, private property and the hacienda order against agrarian radicalism. Anti-communist but suspicious of foreign influence and Guayaquil's commercial liberals, it draws on the highland provinces, the clergy and rural notables, whose patronage still moves votes in the Sierra.

15.name: La Argolla
15.text:
La Argolla, 'the Ring', is what Ecuadorians call the closed circle of banking and agro-export families of Guayaquil, enriched by cacao and the banana boom. Its most powerful figure is the banana magnate Luis Noboa Naranjo, alongside the bankers of the port and the chambers of commerce and agriculture.

They want free trade, low taxes, cheap credit and a weak, compliant state, and resist agrarian reform on the coast and any attempt by Quito to control foreign exchange. Pro-Western and pragmatic, they fund candidates of every party. Their leverage lies in exports, credit and the press of Guayaquil.

16.name: Partido Social Cristiano
16.text:
The Social Christian Party was founded in 1951 by Camilo Ponce Enríquez, who served as president from 1956 to 1960 and ran again in 1968 with Conservative support. It is a modernising party of the right, distinct from the old Conservative Party.

It champions private enterprise, sound money, foreign investment, efficient administration and a firmly pro-American foreign policy, combining Christian social language with business-friendly economics. Its base lies among urban professionals and entrepreneurs in Quito and Guayaquil, and its leverage lies in its links with business and its disciplined deputies in Congress.

17.name: Fundación Charles Darwin para las Islas Galápagos
17.native_full: Fundación Charles Darwin para las Islas Galápagos
17.text:
The Charles Darwin Foundation was established in 1959, the year the Galápagos became Ecuador's first national park, and opened its research station on Santa Cruz Island in 1964. It brings together Ecuadorian and foreign scientists under UNESCO patronage.

It works to save the islands' giant tortoises and unique wildlife from goats, rats and settlers, and urges the government to limit colonisation, fishing and the rising tourist trade. It has no party ties, but its international prestige, scientific authority and foreign funding give it unusual influence over policy toward the archipelago.

18.name: Partido Socialista Revolucionario Ecuatoriano
18.text:
The Revolutionary Socialist Party split from the Ecuadorian Socialist Party in the early 1960s, led by the Marxist intellectual Manuel Agustín Aguirre, a former rector of the Central University. It took with it much of the socialist youth inspired by the Cuban revolution.

It calls for a socialist Ecuador built on worker and peasant power, nationalisation of banks, foreign trade and oil, and solidarity with the Third World, independent of Moscow's line. Its base is in the universities, among teachers and in some unions, and its leverage lies in its intellectual weight on the left.

19.name: Partido Comunista Marxista Leninista del Ecuador
19.native_full: Partido Comunista Marxista Leninista del Ecuador
19.text:
The PCMLE was founded in 1964 by militants who broke with the pro-Soviet Communist Party in the Sino-Soviet split. It operates clandestinely and rejects the electoral road as revisionist.

Following Mao Zedong and Enver Hoxha, it calls for a people's war, a worker-peasant alliance and the overthrow of the landlord and comprador state, denouncing both American imperialism and Soviet 'social-imperialism'. Its strength lies among teachers, students and parts of the FEUE, where its cadres compete fiercely with the PCE for control of student and teachers' organisations.

20.name: Concentración de Fuerzas Populares
20.text:
The Concentration of People's Forces was founded in 1949 by Carlos Guevara Moreno and is now led by Assad Bucaram, a former mayor of Guayaquil and the most popular politician on the coast. It dominates the vote of Guayaquil's suburbs and is widely seen as the likely winner of the next presidential election.

The CFP rails against the oligarchy and the old parties, promising housing, jobs, honest administration and a better share for the poor of the coast. Its message is more personal than ideological. Its leverage lies in its mass following in Guayaquil, which makes the elites and the army fear Bucaram.

21.name: Acción Revolucionaria Nacionalista Ecuatoriana
21.text:
ARNE was founded in 1942 by Jorge Luna Yepes in the aftermath of the territorial loss to Peru, modelled on the Spanish Falange. It has supported Velasco Ibarra at several points and has a presence among Catholic students and the conservative middle class of Quito.

It preaches Catholic nationalism, hierarchy, a corporatist state, Hispanidad and the recovery of the Amazon territories lost in 1941, and is fiercely anti-communist and anti-liberal. Its numbers are small, but its disciplined militants and street squads give it influence in student clashes and right-wing mobilisations.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas del Ecuador
22.text:
The Ecuadorian Armed Forces have repeatedly intervened in politics, most recently governing through the junta of 1963 to 1966. Since Velasco's return they serve as the arbiter of a paralysed political system, and the President depends on their loyalty against Congress, the students and the unions.

The officer corps is anti-communist and trained by the United States, but increasingly nationalist, obsessed with the border dispute with Peru and with the oil now being found in the Amazon. Its leverage is decisive: no president can survive without the army's consent.

23.name: La Nobleza Quiteña
23.text:
The Quito Nobility are the old landowning families of the capital who descend from the colonial aristocracy of the Royal Audiencia of Quito and still cherish Spanish titles, coats of arms and haciendas in the highland valleys.

They look back with nostalgia to the Hispanic Catholic order of the viceroyalty, despise the populism of Velasco and Bucaram, and keep close ties with Spain and its monarchist circles. They have no programme for a crown in Ecuador, but their wealth, marriages and social clubs still shape the Conservative Party and the Quito establishment.
